title: All tremble (129–132)
hookLine: all tremble at the rod, all fear death; putting yourself in their place, do not kill

lines: THE TODDLER AT THE SLAMMED DOOR.
cards: Raise your hand quickly near a dog that's been hit before, and it flinches. Slam a door in a house with a toddler, and the whole small body jumps. A pigeon on the sidewalk scatters when your foot comes down too near.
Nobody taught them that. The flinch comes before any thought. Chapter ten of the Dhammapada is called punishment, and it starts right there, with the flinch that everyone shares.

teach.b: Its Pali name is Daṇḍavagga. A daṇḍa is a stick, a rod, a staff: the thing you're hit with, and so, punishment.
Verse one twenty-nine, in Max Müller's words: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter."
Müller wrote all men, but the Pali word is simply sabbe, all, and some readers hear it as all beings: the dog, the pigeon, the fish on the hook.

At the heart of the verse is a short Pali phrase meaning, roughly, making yourself the comparison. Fear is known from the inside, so your own fear says what it's like for them. No complicated philosophy.
Just your own flinch, turned outward. This is the root of the first precept, the training to refrain from taking life, from camp three. Verse one thirty gives it a gentler turn: "all men love life."
Verses one thirty-one and one thirty-two make the same point about happiness. Everyone, the text says, longs for it.
One who seeks their own happiness by harming beings who also long for happiness, Müller writes, "will not find happiness after death."
One who doesn't harm them will. That's the chapter's method, and it's imagination: before you raise the rod, feel yourself on the other end of it.

how: Buddhist teachers cite these verses as a basis of the first precept, refraining from taking life, which covers animals as well as people; some practitioners carry insects outside rather than kill them.

o: every being fears harm, just as you do
everyone should fear the gods' punishment

games.q: match each word to what it means.
p: a stick or rod, and so punishment

s: the verse only talks about human beings
Müller wrote all men, but the Pali sabbe just means all, and some readers hear all beings.
the verse asks you to use your own fear to understand others

Daṇḍavagga: the chapter of the rod, or punishment.

games.q: a wasp is buzzing at the kitchen window. you have a rolled-up magazine in your hand. what does verse 129 suggest?
o: swat it; it's only a wasp.
picture its fear as your own, and find another way.
leave the room and forget it.
games.why: the verse's method is making yourself the comparison. some Buddhists open the window or carry insects out instead.

practice: Remember a moment when you were afraid, not the worst one, a small one: a near miss in traffic, a raised voice, a letter you dreaded opening, and feel where the fear lived in your body.
Now bring to mind someone else, a person or an animal, who might feel that same flinch today, maybe because of you, maybe not.
For a few breaths, put yourself in their place, let your fear and theirs be the same fear, then rest in the breath.
